The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}+c.$ Find the value of $k-c.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=4,$ hence $c=4.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,6),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=6$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}+4 & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{6})}^{0}+4 & =6 \\ k+4 & =6 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
k-c=2-4=-2.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=2{(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}+4.$
